#Text=To preserve ORANGES or LEMONS. [18th]
#Text=
#Text=Take seville oranges, the largest and roughest you can get, clear of
#Text=spots, chip them very fine, and put them into water for two days,
#Text=shifting them twice or three times a day, then boil them whilst they
#Text=are soft: take and cut them into quarters, and take out all the pippens
#Text=with a penknife, so weigh them, and to every pound of orange, take a
#Text=pound and half of loaf sugar; put your sugar into a pan, and to every
#Text=pound of sugar a pint of water, set it over the fire to melt, and when
#Text=it boils skim it very well, then put in your oranges; if you would have
#Text=any of them whole, make a little hole at the top, and take out the meat
#Text=with a tea spoon, set your oranges over a slow fire to boil, and keep
#Text=them skimming all the while; keep your oranges as much as you can with
#Text=the skin downwards; you may cover them with a delf-plate, to bear them
#Text=down in the boiling; let them boil for three quarters of an hour, then
#Text=put them into a pot or bason, and let them stand two days covered, then
#Text=boil them again whilst they look clear, and the syrrup be thick, so put
#Text=them into a pot, and lie close over them a paper dip'd in brandy, and
#Text=tie a double paper at the top, set them in a cool place, and keep them
#Text=for use.
#Text=If you would have your oranges that are whole to look pale and
#Text=clear, to put in glasses, you must make a syrrup of pippen jelly; then
#Text=take ten or a dozen pippens, as they are of bigness, pare and slice
#Text=them, and boil them in as much water as will cover them till they be
#Text=thoroughly tender, so strain your water from the pippens through a hair
#Text=sieve, then strain it through a flannel bag; and to every pint of jelly
#Text=take a pound of double refined sugar, set it over a fire to boil, and
#Text=skim it, let it boil whilst it be thick, then put it into a pot and
#Text=cover it, but they will keep best if they be put every one in different
#Text=pots.
#Text=To make ONION SOOP [18th]
#Text=
#Text=Take four or five large onions, pill and boil them in milk and water
#Text=whilst tender, (shifting them two or three times in the boiling) beat
#Text='em in a marble mortar to a pulp, and rub them thro' a hair-sieve, and
#Text=put them into a little sweet gravy; then fry a few slices of veal, and
#Text=two or three slices of lean bacon; beat them in a marble mortar as
#Text=small as forc'd-meat; put it into your stew-pan with the gravy and
#Text=onions, and boil them; mi
#Text= a spoonful of wheat-flour with a little
#Text=water, and put it into the soop to keep it from running; strain all
#Text=through a cullender, season it to your taste; then put into the dish a
#Text=little spinage stew'd in butter, and a little crisp bread; so serve it
#Text=up.
#Text=BROWN MIXTURE FOR A COUGH [19th]
#Text=
#Text=Mix in a large bottle, half an ounce of
#Text=liquorice; a quarter of an ounce of gum-arabic; two tea-spoonfuls of
#Text=antimonial wine; sixty drops of laudanum; and half a pint of water.
#Text=Shake it well, and when the ingredients are thoroughly amalgamated it
#Text=will be fit for use.
#Text=For a cold and cough, take a dessert-spoonful three
#Text=or four times a day, shaking or stirring it first.
#Text=LEMON MACCAROONS [19th]
#Text=
#Text=Take four large ripe lemons, and rub off the yellow
#Text=surface of the rind, upon a lump of sugar.
#Text=Then powder that sugar, and
#Text=add to it not quite a pound of loaf-sugar, already powdered.
#Text=Break four
#Text=eggs into a shallow pan, and beat them till very thick and light.
#Text=Then
#Text=add the juice of the lemons, squeezed through a strainer, and a
#Text=tea-spoonful of powdered nutmeg and cinnamon, and stir in the sugar, a
#Text=little at a time, alternately with three large heaped-up table-spoonfuls
#Text=of sifted flour.
#Text=A little more flour may, probably, be found necessary.
#Text=Mix the whole, thoroughly, so as to form a soft paste.
#Text=Have ready some
#Text=shallow, square baking-pans, or sheets of iron, the bottoms covered with
#Text=white paper, laid smoothly in.
#Text=Moisten your hands with water, and then
#Text=take up portions of the mixture, and roll them into balls, about the
#Text=size of a large plum, laying them, as you proceed, upon the paper, but
#Text=rather more than an inch apart.
#Text=Lastly, with the blade of a knife,
#Text=dipped in water, smooth the surface of each.
#Text=Set them into a moderate
#Text=oven, and bake them brown.
#Text=Try one, when you think they are done.
#Text=If not
#Text=sufficiently baked, let them remain longer in the oven.
#Text=As soon as they
#Text=are cold, loosen them from the paper, by slipping under them a
#Text=broad-bladed knife.
#Text=Orange maccaroons may be made in this manner, using
#Text=the grated rind of two oranges only, but the juice of four.
#Text=To make
#Text=vanilla maccaroons, boil, in a covered vessel, a vanilla bean, with as
#Text=much milk as will barely cover it.
#Text=When the milk is strongly flavoured
#Text=with the vanilla, strain it, and, when cold, add it to the beaten egg.
#Text=Then stir in, gradually, the sugar, spice, and flour, and proceed as
#Text=above.
#Text=Baked Apples and Nuts. [20th]
#Text=
#Text=For a half dozen large apples a good
#Text=three-fourths cup of nut meats, butternuts, black walnuts or hickory
#Text=nuts--will be required.
#Text=Chop the meats fine and add a half cup of sugar.
#Text=Core the apples and fill the centres with the nuts and sugar.
#Text=Put in a
#Text=rather deep pan, with a cupful of boiling water added, bag and bake.
#Text=When tender remove carefully, place in a pretty dish, pour the juice
#Text=over the apples, and crown with whipped cream or a meringue made from
#Text=the whites of two eggs.
#Text=Rye Bread Pudding. [20th]
#Text=
#Text=Toast stale rye bread to a golden brown, then roll
#Text=into fine crumbs.
#Text=Brush small custard cups or a mould with melted
#Text=butter, sprinkle over a few currants, raisins, prunes (cut fine) or
#Text=figs, then fill with crumbs.
#Text=Beat three eggs without separating until
#Text=light, add three tablespoonfuls of sugar, a pint of milk (with vanilla
#Text=or nutmeg to flavor) and pour carefully over the bread crumbs.
#Text=Let them
#Text=stand ten minutes, until the mixture has soaked into the crumbs; then
#Text=set in a paper bag in a pan of cold water and cook like a custard in the
#Text=oven.
#Text=It will take about half an hour.
#Text=Test by slipping the blade of the
#Text=knife down the side of the bag.
#Text=If it comes up clear, the pudding is
#Text=sufficiently baked.
#Text=Serve hot with lemon or egg sauce or fruit syrup.
#Text=Tapioca Apple Pudding. [20th]
#Text=
#Text=Soak one cupful tapioca in three pints cold water over night.
#Text=In the morning put on to boil and cook twenty or thirty minutes,
#Text=until it looks clear.
#Text=Add a quart and a half peeled and
#Text=quartered apples, one cup of sugar, a teaspoonful salt, and lemon juice
#Text=or extract to flavor.
#Text=Turn into a buttered dish, put in bag and bake an
#Text=hour in a moderate oven.
#Text=When cold serve with cream and sugar.
